title: IEEE 1500: wrapping cores
summary: An SoC is built from **cores** — processors, interfaces, accelerators — often designed by different teams or bought from vendors. IEEE 1500 puts a standard **wrapper** around each core so it can be tested on its own, with its own tests, and so the wiring between cores can be tested too. This topic goes through the wrapper's interface signal by signal.
objectives: Explain why cores in an SoC need their own test wrappers.
Name the parts of an IEEE 1500 wrapper and its serial-port signals.
Describe a wrapper boundary cell and its modes.
Explain the standard instructions and which register each puts between WSI and WSO.
Describe the parallel port and how wrappers are controlled and documented in an SoC.

blocks.md: A core vendor ships the core **with its test patterns**. Inside an SoC, however, the core's terminals are not chip pins — they are connected to other logic. To reuse the patterns, the core must be **isolated** from its neighbours and reachable by the tester. That is the job of the IEEE 1500 wrapper: it does for a core what boundary scan does for a chip.

blocks.caption: Three wrapped cores: a serial path WSI → WSO through all wrappers, control from the TAP, and a wide parallel port for one core

blocks.title: Divide and conquer
blocks.md: Test each core in isolation (**inward-facing**), then test the wires between cores (**outward-facing**). Patterns are generated core by core — smaller problems for ATPG — and cores can be tested in parallel.

blocks.md: The wrapper has **no state machine** of its own. Instead of TMS, it receives the decoded control signals directly — the chip-level controller (usually the TAP) produces them.

spots.title: Functional path CFI → CFO
spots.md: **C**ell **F**unctional **I**nput and **O**utput. In functional mode the signal passes straight through the output mux — the core works normally.

spots.title: Capture
spots.md: In a capture, the value on CFI is loaded into the cell. For a core **input** cell this observes what the neighbouring logic sends — used in outward-facing (EXTEST) tests.

spots.title: Capture / shift mux
spots.md: Chooses what the flip-flop loads: the value on **CFI** (capture) or the bit from the previous cell on **CTI** (shift). **C**ell **T**est **I**nput and **O**utput connect the cells into the WBR chain between WSI and WSO.

spots.title: Shift flip-flop
spots.md: Clocked by WRCK while ShiftWR or CaptureWR is active.

spots.title: Update / hold stage
spots.md: Holds a stable value while the chain shifts, so the core input does not see moving bits. Some cells have no separate update stage; then the shift flip-flop drives directly.

spots.title: Output mux
spots.md: In inward-facing test mode the cell — not CFI — drives the core input (CFO): the core is **controlled** and isolated from its neighbours.

rows: **drives** the wire to the next core
blocks.caption: What a cell does in each mode

items.title: Dedicated and shared cells
items.md: A **dedicated** cell adds its own flip-flop. A **shared** cell reuses a functional flip-flop that already sits at the core boundary — less area and no extra delay on the functional path, but the cell's behaviour then depends on the core's design.

items.title: Which terminals get cells?
items.md: Normally every functional input and output. **Clocks**, asynchronous resets and analog signals usually do not; they are documented as exceptions.

items.title: Why a safe state?
items.md: While one core is tested, its outputs must not disturb running neighbours. Safe values keep the wires quiet — for example, *not* asserting a write enable into a neighbour's memory.

blocks.caption: IEEE 1500 instructions: WS_ = serial port, WP_ = parallel port

steps.title: Loading the WIR
steps.md: With **SelectWIR = 1** the WIR is between WSI and WSO, and the instruction is shifted in.

steps.title: WS_BYPASS
steps.md: With SelectWIR = 0 the instruction chooses the data register. WS_BYPASS: only the 1-bit **WBY** — the core works normally and adds one bit to the path.

steps.title: WS_EXTEST
steps.md: The **WBR** is on the path; its cells drive and capture the wires **outside** the core.

steps.title: WS_INTEST_SCAN
steps.md: The WBR and the core's internal **scan chains** form one long path. The vendor's scan patterns are applied to the isolated core.

blocks.caption: Through the WPP several chains are shifted at once

blocks.md:
The serial port moves one bit per clock — fine for instructions and small tests, far too slow for the millions of scan bits of a large core. The optional **wrapper parallel port** connects the WBR segments and the core's internal chains to several chip-level **scan pins** (or a test bus), so many chains shift at once. Its width and use are chosen by the SoC integrator.

In the SoC, the **WSC signals** come from the chip's TAP: the TAP states produce *ShiftWR*, *CaptureWR*, *UpdateWR*, and a TAP instruction (or an IJTAG network, Topic 6) puts the wrappers on the scan path.

items.title: CTL: documenting a wrapped core
items.md: A wrapped core is delivered with a description in **CTL** — the Core Test Language, IEEE 1450.6. It tells the SoC integrator the wrapper's instructions, its terminals, its scan chains and how the core's test patterns must be applied.

items.title: Compliant and unwrapped cores
items.md: A *1500-compliant* core comes with its wrapper. A *1500-ready* (unwrapped) core comes without one but with the CTL information needed to add a wrapper during SoC integration.

items.title: 1500 and 1687 together
items.md: IEEE 1500 standardises **what a core looks like** from outside; IEEE 1687 standardises **how instruments are reached** through a network. Real SoCs use both: wrapped cores whose wrapper registers and internal instruments sit inside an IJTAG network.
